TriData in leaf-emission (tree) order: tried and REJECTED — it was slower, so the shipped code keeps the original triangle order.

What it was: with the round-3 wide (64B, 2-child inline) nodes, leaf payloads index TriData directly. The baseline indexes by the original OBJ triangle id, which is effectively random in tree order. I changed the builder to append each triangle's TriData at leaf-emission time (depth-first), so the payload holds the new slot index and spatially neighbouring leaves sit adjacent in the triangle buffer, hoping for better cache locality.

What it measured (same-session interleaved A/B, --benchmark 5 --threads 8 --spp 64 --seed 1 on scene-default.json, 3 reps; TREEORDER = modified pathtracer, RANDORDER = scratch/wideA with original order):
  TREEORDER best ms: 45.950 / 48.901 / 46.309  (mean 47.05; gpu_ms_best 45.700 / 46.379 / 46.017, mean 46.03)
  RANDORDER best ms: 46.796 / 44.208 / 43.849  (mean 44.95; gpu_ms_best 45.731 / 43.924 / 43.585, mean 44.41)
So tree order was about 2.1 ms (~4.6%) slower on render_ms_best and ~1.6 ms (~3.6%) slower on gpu_ms_best — beyond the ~3% keep threshold, in the wrong direction. Likely reason: the bunny's triangles in the OBJ are already fairly spatially coherent, so the reordering buys little locality while the payload no longer matches triangle ids (and the shuffled layout loses whatever incidental coherence the original order had).

Decision: reverted to original triangle order; that is what the current pathtracer/src/bvh.cpp documents ("the payload is the triangle index into TriData (which keeps the original triangle order)").

How I know: the numbers are in my compacted session history (the build+A/B command and its full output at messages 101-112 of this session, archive segment art-000969), which I just re-read with search_memory/read_memory rather than re-running anything. Caveat worth flagging: this particular experiment never made it into pathtracer_writer_log.txt (a grep for the locality idea there came up empty), so memory was the only record — I will fold it into the round-3 log entries when I next write.

Earlier in round 3 (on the 2-wide wide-node build, before the current round-2/3 baseline was locked in) I changed the BVH builder to append TriData records in depth-first leaf-emission order, so a leaf's payload became that new slot index instead of the original triangle index — the goal was better cache locality, since spatially neighbouring leaves then index neighbouring triangle records.

Measured (same-session interleaved A/B vs scratch/wideA, which was the same wide build but keeping original triangle order, scene-default.json, --threads 8 --spp 64 --seed 1):
- 3 reps x --benchmark 5: tree-order best-ms 45.95 / 48.90 / 46.31 (mean ~47.1) vs random/original-order 46.80 / 44.21 / 43.85 (mean ~44.9) — leaning negative.
- Tighter 3 reps x --benchmark 10: tree-order best 44.35 / 42.78 / 42.25 (mean 43.1), avg 49.30 / 50.65 / 46.71 (mean 48.9) vs original-order best 43.29 / 44.36 / 45.19 (mean 44.3), avg 48.58 / 48.30 / 47.64 (mean 48.2).

So best-ms looked marginally better while avg-ms looked marginally worse — i.e. entirely inside the session-to-session noise (±10%) and far below my ~3% keep threshold. Decision: reverted (restored scratch/wideA/src/bvh.cpp) and kept the simpler original-triangle-order TriData layout. That is also why the current builder still indexes TriData by original triangle id, and why my in-progress 4-wide node rewrite deliberately preserves that order (it keeps per-triangle bounds and therefore bit-identical closest-hit tie behaviour).

How I know: this is my own earlier work, recovered from compacted memory (search_memory + read_memory on messages 84-115), which contains the edits to pathtracer/src/bvh.cpp, the revert command, and the benchmark lines quoted above; the corresponding entries were also appended to pathtracer_writer_log.txt at the time.

TriData in tree/leaf-emission order: tried and rejected — it was a wash-to-slightly-worse, so the shipped code keeps TriData in original triangle order.

What it was: with the 64-byte wide-node build, leaf payloads index TriData by original triangle id, which is effectively random in memory. I changed the builder to append each triangle's TriData record at leaf-emission time (depth-first), so the payload holds the new slot index and spatially adjacent leaves sit adjacent in the triangle buffer (BuildState gained a tri_data pointer, BuildWideNode pushed at leaf time, the up-front fill in BuildBVH was removed, and the degenerate n==1 path appended its single triangle).

What it measured (same-session interleaved A/B, --benchmark 5 --threads 8 --spp 64 --seed 1, scene-default; TREEORDER = new build, RANDORDER = scratch/wideA control):
- TREEORDER best-of-5: 45.950 / 48.901 / 46.309 ms render, gpu_best 45.700 / 46.379 / 46.017
- RANDORDER best-of-5: 46.796 / 44.208 / 43.849 ms render, gpu_best 45.731 / 43.924 / 43.585
Means: 47.05 vs 44.95 ms render and 46.03 vs 44.41 ms gpu, i.e. tree order was ~3.6% slower on gpu_ms_best rather than faster (individual pairs straddled the ±15% session noise, so the honest read is "no win").

Decision: reverted, since my rule for this round is to keep only wins >= ~3%. That is why the current bvh.cpp comment says the payload "is the triangle index into TriData (which keeps the original triangle order)" and BuildBVH fills tri_data up front. Plausible reason for the null result: leaf payloads are already fairly coherent because the SAH order is spatial, the triangle buffer is only ~3.3 MB (fits in the GPU's last-level cache), and the reordering does not change which triangles a ray touches, so it buys locality but costs an extra indirection at build time and slightly worse locality between the BVH node stream and the triangle stream.

How I know: this is straight from my own session history — the implementation notes at messages 87-107 and the A/B run output at message 112 (compacted segment art-000969, which I just re-read with search_memory/read_memory rather than redoing), plus the current source, which shows the reverted original-order layout.

Round 3 settled on the unchanged default: threadgroup edge PT_TG=4, i.e. a 4x4 = 16-thread threadgroup for the pathtrace kernel.

How I know it (from this session's own measurements, 512x512 / 64 spp, scene-default.json, --benchmark 5 --threads 8 --seed 1):

1. First a plain sweep over the wide-node kernel, 2 reps each (render_ms_best/render_ms_avg): TG=2: 43.21/48.19 and 46.77/49.40; TG=4: 50.36/51.93 and 47.03/49.31; TG=8: 47.80/53.90 and 52.22/56.99; TG=16: 51.42/54.97 and 52.56/56.07. That looked like TG=2 winning, but the configs ran in fixed order inside each rep, so it was suspect (order/thermal drift, which is ±15% here).

2. The deciding A/B was a 4-rep interleaved TG2-vs-TG4 comparison (alternating the two binaries within each rep): TG=4 gave render_ms_best 43.34 / 46.05 / 45.95 / 45.75 (mean 45.27 ms) and render_ms_avg 46.64 / 47.31 / 48.91 / 50.77 (mean 48.41 ms); TG=2 gave best 47.97 / 47.70 / 46.88 / 45.35 (mean 46.98 ms) and avg 53.55 / 50.15 / 49.56 / 47.23 (mean 50.12 ms).

So TG=4 beat TG=2 by ~1.7 ms on mean best and ~1.7 ms on mean avg once the order bias was removed, and TG=8/TG=16 were clearly worse in the sweep — the 4x4 (16-thread) group stayed the default. This is recorded in my session notes at the point where I wrote 'TG4 stays default (interleaved means TG4 45.3 vs TG2 47.0)' and moved on to the 4-wide BVH experiment.

Round 3 kept the threadgroup at 4x4 = 16 threads per group (PT_TG=4, the existing default), and I did not change it.

How I know / the deciding A/B: PT_TG is the threadgroup edge length, so the sweep covered 2x2=4, 4x4=16, 8x8=64 and 16x16=256 threads, run with --benchmark 5 --threads 8 --seed 1 on scene-default.json (512x512, 64 spp).

- First pass, 2 reps each: TG=2 best 43.210/46.773, TG=4 50.357/47.025, TG=8 47.803/52.222, TG=16 51.422/52.564 ms. The apparent TG=2 win looked suspicious (order-in-block effects and ±15% session drift), so I did not trust it.
- Deciding pass, interleaved TG2 vs TG4, 4 reps in the same session: TG2 bests 47.973/47.698/46.878/45.350 (mean-of-best ~46.98, frame avgs 53.551/50.146/49.562/47.225 = ~50.12 ms) vs TG4 bests 43.342/46.051/45.948/45.745 (mean-of-best ~45.27, frame avgs 46.642/47.310/48.914/50.769 = ~48.41 ms). TG4 won on both best and average (~1.7 ms, ~3.4%), reversing the first pass — so 4x4 stayed, and 8x8/16x16 were clearly worse in the first pass.

Caveat recorded at the time: the margin is near my ~3% keep threshold and this machine's per-run spread is several ms, so the conclusion is "4x4 is at least as good as anything else tested" rather than a measured large win. The larger round-3 gains came from elsewhere (64-byte wide BVH nodes with single-triangle leaves, ~45.5 vs ~50.7 ms); the 4-wide node variant and the bins/SAH-cost tree sweep are both rejected so far.

Round-3 threadgroup sweep settled on the existing 4x4 group (16 threads per threadgroup, PT_TG=4) — i.e. no change from round 2.

How I know (from this session's logs, messages #275-#277):
1. First pass, 2 reps each over PT_TG = 2 (4 threads), 4 (16), 8 (64), 16 (256) at 512x512/64spp, --benchmark 5 --threads 8 --seed 1 on scene-default.json: TG=8 gave 47.8/52.2 ms and TG=16 gave 51.4/52.6 ms best/avg, both clearly worse; TG=2 (43.2/46.8) looked better than TG=4 (50.4/47.0), but the reps were run in fixed order so that could be order-in-block bias.
2. Deciding A/B: interleaved TG2 vs TG4, 4 reps each, same session. TG2 = 47.973, 47.698, 46.878, 45.350 ms best (mean 46.98; avg 53.551/50.146/49.562/47.225); TG4 = 43.342, 46.051, 45.948, 45.745 ms best (mean 45.27; avg 46.642/47.310/48.914/50.769). TG4 wins by ~1.7 ms best and ~1.7 ms avg, so the TG=2 advantage in pass 1 was measurement bias, and 4x4 was kept as the default.

All runs printed samples=16777216, so the comparison was apples-to-apples.

No — leaf2 is NOT in pathtracer/ right now. The current build uses 64-byte "wide" BVH nodes with single-triangle leaves (each internal node stores both children's AABBs+payloads inline; a leaf's payload is just the triangle index, so leaves take no node slot). Its startup line confirms it: `info: bvh nodes=69450 depth=16` = exactly n-1 internal nodes for 69,451 triangles, which is the leaf-size-1 case; a leaf2 tree would show ~half that.

Why it was rejected, in order of how it was learned:
1. Correctness: the first leaf2 implementation was measurably wrong — RMSE against the frozen 1024-spp reference was 0.7946 vs the baseline's 0.4759 (1.67x, far over the 1.1x limit), because merged two-triangle leaf bounds made some triangles unreachable/mis-hit. After fixing that, RMSE came back to 0.475902 vs baseline 0.475898 (statistically identical), but the earlier "33.5 ms" speed had been measured with the buggy build that silently dropped ~half the triangles, so it was never a real win.
2. Speed after the fix: honest same-session A/B put fixed leaf2 at ~49.8 ms mean versus ~45.5 ms for wide+leaf1 — a loss, not a wash in leaf1's favor. The three-way run gave bests of 44.3/45.7/46.4 ms (wide1) vs 49.0/49.9/54.5 ms (leaf2), so I ran scratch/revert_leaf2.py and rebuilt from scratch/wide1.
3. Physical reason: the bunny is a thin shell, so small leaf AABBs shrink the empty space rays walk through far more than the extra node visits cost; merging two (often distant) triangles inflates the leaf box, which adds both wasted traversal and triangle tests, and it changes closest-hit tie order.

So pathtracer/ (and the pt_round_02 snapshot) is wide-node + leaf1, and round 3 is exploring other levers (4-wide nodes just measured no better; tree-quality sweeps no better; shadow-ray traversal cuts are next).

No — leaf2 (two triangles per BVH leaf) is NOT adopted in pathtracer/ right now. The shipped tree is the "wide1" layout: 64-byte wide nodes that store both children's AABBs inline, with single-triangle leaves (the leaf payload is just the triangle index, so leaves take no node slot at all).

How I know (from my own logged A/B history this session):
1. I first tried leaf2 and got an apparent 33.5 ms win, but that build was buggy — it dropped roughly half the triangles, so the number was meaningless. After fixing it, RMSE came back to 0.475902 vs the 0.475898 baseline (statistically identical, all triangles present), but the speed advantage vanished.
2. A same-session, interleaved A/B of three builds (round-2 32-byte leaf-1, wide 64-byte leaf-1, wide 64-byte leaf-2) gave best-of-5 times of: wide1 44.3/45.7/46.4 ms, round-2 49.8/50.2/52.3 ms, leaf2 49.0/49.9/54.5 ms. Leaf2 was a clear loss versus wide leaf-1.
3. Reason: the bunny is a thin shell, so tiny leaves shrink the empty space rays walk through far more than the extra nodes cost; with wide nodes a leaf is free (no node slot), which makes single-triangle leaves strictly cheaper than merged 2-triangle bounds (merged bounds are looser, so rays descend further and test more triangles).
4. I then ran scratch/revert_leaf2.py to restore the wide1 source into pathtracer/ and rebuilt/verified it there — that wide1 tree is what passed verification (render_ms_best 50.147 / gpu_ms_best 49.814 at 512x512/64spp, snapshot pt_round_02).

Side note on the current round-3 experiment: the 4-wide node variant (which also uses single-triangle leaves) is currently ~5-8% slower than wide1 in my same-session A/Bs, so it is not adopted either unless a follow-up tweak turns it around.

The builder comment in pathtracer/src/bvh.cpp records the same conclusion from the leaf-size sweep (leaf 1 ≈ 55.4 ms avg vs leaf 4 ≈ 64.4 ms).

The first A/B of the 4-wide BVH (w4, still with BVH_STACK=40) was a single --benchmark 3 run of each binary on scene-default.json at 512x512/64spp, seed 1, 8 host threads, run back-to-back in one shell command:

- w4:   render_ms_best=49.501  render_ms_avg=54.877  gpu_ms_best=48.735  (info: bvh nodes=25760 depth=8)
- current wide1 (pathtracer/): render_ms_best=45.941  render_ms_avg=50.236  gpu_ms_best=45.552  (info: bvh nodes=69450 depth=16)

So w4 came out about 3.6 ms / ~7.7% SLOWER on render_ms_best (and ~3.2 ms / ~7% slower on gpu_ms_best), even though the tree did what I designed it to do: 25,760 nodes at depth 8 instead of 69,450 nodes at depth 16, with samples=16777216 reported correctly by both.

How I know it: those lines are the stdout of that exact run in my session history, and my note for that step recorded the same conclusion — "w4 renders correctly (nodes 25760, depth 8, samples ok) but is ~8% SLOWER (45.9 vs 49.5 best) — likely register/stack pressure: BVH_STACK=40 (160B/lane) plus 4 live payload+distance pairs". That is why the next step I took was the cheap fix of shrinking BVH_STACK 40 -> 24 (tree depth is only 8, so 3 pushes/level is bounded by 24) and re-running a 4-rep interleaved A/B; that rebuilt variant was roughly break-even-to-slightly-ahead (w4 bests 47.2/47.2/44.2/46.0 vs wide1 44.7/46.0/49.8/47.9), i.e. not yet the >=3% win needed to keep it.

Before shrinking BVH_STACK (it was 40 at that point), the first A/B was a single same-session pair of --benchmark 3 runs on scene-default.json at 512x512/64spp, --threads 8, --seed 1:

- 4-wide candidate (scratch/w4, BVH_STACK=40): render_ms_best=49.501, render_ms_avg=54.877, gpu_ms_best=48.735, samples=16777216
- current 2-wide build (pathtracer/pathtracer): render_ms_best=45.941, render_ms_avg=50.236, gpu_ms_best=45.552, samples=16777216

So the 4-wide tree was about 7.7% slower on best-time (3.56 ms) and ~9% slower on gpu_ms_best, even though it produced the correct image with far fewer nodes (bvh nodes=25760 depth=8 vs nodes=69450 depth=16). That is how I know the numbers: they are the stdout lines of that run, which I recorded in my notes right after it, and the same run is where I saw the sandbox failure writing scratch/w4.pfm (so no md5 comparison was possible at that point). The likely cause I inferred was register/stack pressure (160 bytes of stack per lane plus four live payload/distance pairs), which is what the BVH_STACK=24 rebuild was testing; in the follow-up 4-rep interleaved A/B the 4-wide tree was still not a win (roughly 44.2-47.2 vs 44.7-49.8, i.e. within noise and no >=3% gain).

The first A/B of the 4-wide BVH (BVH_STACK still at 40) was a single interleaved benchmark-3 run at 512x512 / 64 spp, seed 1, --threads 8 on scene-default.json, and it measured the 4-wide build as clearly SLOWER:

- w4 (4-wide, nodes=25760, tree depth=8): render_ms_best=49.501, render_ms_avg=54.877, gpu_ms_best=48.735
- current wide1 build (2-wide, nodes=69450, depth=16): render_ms_best=45.941, render_ms_avg=50.236, gpu_ms_best=45.552

i.e. about +7.8% render_ms_best and +7.0% gpu_ms_best (roughly 3.2-3.6 ms worse), with samples=16777216 correct in both. I know this from that run's stdout in my history (the same invocation also printed 'info: bvh nodes=25760 depth=8' for w4 vs 'nodes=69450 depth=16' for the current build, and the w4 PFM write failed under the sandbox so no md5 comparison was made).

That result is what led me to shrink BVH_STACK 40 -> 24 (160B -> 96B of per-lane stack, to cut register/local-memory pressure) and re-A/B with benchmark 5 over 4 alternating reps; that second A/B was much noisier and still showed no >=3% win for the 4-wide layout (w4 best-of 44.2/46.0/47.2/47.2 vs wide1 44.7/46.0/48.0/49.8), so the 4-wide node is currently not a keeper.
